system_map.overview: The repository shows an agent-execution system organised around a central FlowRunner, an LLM provider abstraction using LiteLLM and a mock client, governance action engines, compliance evaluation, and typed steering models. Orchestration appears centralized rather than multi-agent, with persistent knowledge, runtime context, and CI workflows supporting governance and traceability.

orchestration.description: Execution appears to pass through a single FlowRunner entry point, with governance and compliance engines acting as centralized control and evaluation guards rather than peer agents.

patterns.name: LLM Provider Abstraction

tool_protocols.notes: No MCP or explicit tool-calling protocol evidence appears in the provided symbols.

optimisation_targets.notes: The mock client supports offline execution and avoids live LLM cost during development or tests.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Provider abstraction preserves execution simplicity while allowing different LLM backends to be swapped.

patterns.summary: LLM calls are abstracted into separate LiteLLM and mock client modules, isolating model providers from flow execution.
patterns.intent: Separate LLM provider concerns from flow logic so execution can be tested, rerun, or switched between real and deterministic model clients.
patterns.context: Present in the LLM package used by the CAS runner, with LiteLLM declared as a project dependency.
forces: Live LLM availability must not block deterministic execution.
Real and mock client semantics must remain aligned to avoid fake test success.
Prompt and response handling must survive provider changes.
patterns.solution: Two client implementations are provided: LiteLLMClient for real provider access and MockLLMClient for deterministic or offline behaviour. The runner can depend on a client boundary rather than a specific model vendor.
implementation_signals: Client classes named LiteLLMClient and MockLLMClient.

evidence.note: Defines a real-provider LLM client.
Defines a mock LLM client for deterministic execution.
Declares litellm as a runtime dependency.

benefits: Provider portability.
Offline and CI-friendly execution.
Easier testing of flow logic independent of model latency or failure.
costs: Client contracts must be maintained in parallel.
Mock behaviour can become an inaccurate stand-in for real LLM responses.
failure_modes: The mock client may hide prompt, schema, or tooling issues that only surface with a real LLM.
Divergent request/response handling can make provider switching unreliable.

patterns.reuse_notes: Useful for any LLM pipeline that needs deterministic tests or provider portability. Keep the mock client contractually close to the real client, especially for structured outputs.

forces: Execution order must be explicit.
Errors and governance checks need a common stopping point.
Distributed agent autonomy is not evidenced, so central control keeps behaviour predictable.
patterns.solution: FlowRunner is used as the main runtime executor, invoked through the CLI and supported by orchestration and execution-sequence documentation.
implementation_signals: CLI main entry point in cli.py.
Architecture documents named cas-orchestration-flow.md and cas-execution-sequence.md.

evidence.note: Defines the central execution runner.
Provides the CLI entry point that likely invokes the runner.
Architecture document path indicates an orchestration flow design.
Architecture document path indicates an execution sequence design.

benefits: Clear execution sequence.
Simpler observability and debugging.
Easier enforcement of governance at a central boundary.

optimisation_targets.notes: Allowed transitions are explicit, reducing uncontrolled state mutation.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: State changes are restricted to registered transitions, reducing autonomous variation.

patterns.summary: GovernanceActionEngine uses a TransitionRegistry to enforce allowed governed state transitions.
patterns.intent: Prevent arbitrary state changes by encoding which transitions are valid for governance actions.
patterns.context: Found in the governance package alongside GovernanceAction and related governance models.
forces: Governance state must remain auditable.
Invalid transitions should be rejected rather than repaired ad hoc.
Explicit rules are easier to test than implicit behavioural assumptions.
patterns.solution: TransitionRegistry holds registered transitions, while GovernanceActionEngine applies actions through those transitions.

evidence.note: Shows a registry-based state transition mechanism tied to a governance action engine.
Defines the action type that can be transitioned or evaluated.

benefits: Deterministic state behaviour.
Clear audit trail of allowed moves.
Easier reasoning about governance safety.
costs: New workflows must be registered explicitly.
The registry can become a maintenance surface as governance semantics grow.
failure_modes: Missing transitions block valid actions.
Overly broad transitions weaken the governance guarantee.

patterns.reuse_notes: Use for any agent system where LLM or tool actions must move governed objects through a finite state model. Keep transitions data-driven if possible.

patterns.reuse_notes: Use when an agent system needs to remember learned or discovered capabilities without treating every claim as permanent truth.

patterns.reuse_notes: Use in any system where automated agents or workflows can modify or create CI definitions. Treat workflow definitions as part of the agent contract and validate them deterministically.
